item.title: Tories welcome Louise Haigh’s hint government could adopt their plan to scrap Natural England – UK politics live
item.description: First secretary of state has declined to say whether Natural England will be abolished as part of plans to cut the number of quangos Natural England could be abolished as part of quango cull, says Louise Haigh Q: Can you confirm that, under the SPS deal announced on Friday, MPs won’t be able to vote down any new regulations on food and drink standards? Haigh did not challenge that assertion from the FT’s Lucy Fisher. But she said that, under the deal, the UK would get “a seat at the table” when EU laws were being drawn up. “We will be consulted on every stage of the legislation,” she said. The problem with this lifetime framing is it makes us all wonder when we’re going to die, and compete with each other in the cabinet. I’m going to abide by collective responsibility in that and say it’s a question for the manifesto. Continue reading...

item.title: The worst COP ever? Climate talks collapse in chaos
item.description: The COP31 climate talks ended in failure Sunday as a contentious deal collapsed over fossil fuels and the summit in Turkey stretched into record overtime. The final agreement was rejected in a chaotic finale to a UN climate summit that ran two days over schedule, underscoring the strains on diplomacy in an increasingly fractured world. France 24’s Douglas Herbert takes a look at whether the failure to reach an agreement makes COP31 the most disappointing climate summit to date.

item.description: Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news Shares in UK housebuilder Crest Nicholson have slumped by a quarter, to a record low, after the company issued a profits warning this morning. Full year completions were 1,353, at the bottom end of the Group’s previous guidance range of 1,350 to 1,400 completions. The warning has hammered Crest Nicholson shares, which have lost more than a quarter of their value this morning, currently trading down over 30%. The brutal sell-off is also weighing on the wider sector, dragging peers like Barratt Redrow, Persimmon, Vistry and Bellway into the red. Today’s update suggests that weakness in the housing market is no longer confined to first-time buyers. Crest Nicholson is predominantly exposed to the mid-premium family housing market, and the sharp deterioration in sales rates indicates that more affluent upsizers are also becoming increasingly cautious amid macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainty. Continue reading...

item.title: ‘One area of the tent was known as fart corner’: what it’s really like to be on The Great British Bake Off
item.description: As we come to the end of another series, former contestants including Kim-Joy, Syabira Yusoff and Christiaan de Vries reminisce on their time in the tent – and the aftermath The Great British Bake Off is just about to finish its best season in years. Like a cloud of Swiss meringue buttercream on a slightly sunken cake, Nigella Lawson has added glamour and indulgence to a format that needed saving. But this year’s contestants have brought the joy, too: talented, charismatic individuals who have interrupted their lives to spend three months with bits of dough stuck to their elbows and indigestion from all the recipe testing. We spoke to five previous contestants to find out why they put themselves through it, and what they feel they achieved in the process. The scale runs from “a very nice level of X-list celebrity” to “a better version of me”, with a lot of life lessons (and a fart corner) along the way. Continue reading...

item.title: Who Is Still Alive review – grief-stricken stories of the places and people lost in Gaza
item.description: Nicolas Wadimoff invites refugees to draw a floor plan of their former neighbourhood, bringing raw and agonising pain to the surface A sombre documentary from the Swiss musician and film-maker Nicolas Wadimoff, who returns to his longstanding interest in Gaza. In this film, a group of survivor-refugees who made it out of Gaza and into Egypt during the bombing gather in an enclosed studio and are invited to draw out a kind of floor plan of what they remember of their neighbourhood. First, this is on paper and then on the studio floor itself; they use that as a basis for their memories of what and who they have lost. (The people who have died are described as having been “martyred”.) The result is almost unbearably painful. The raw and agonising grief, which perhaps stays just at the waterline of consciousness most of the time, is here brought above the surface. They are people suffering from trauma, carrying videos on their phones of their lost loved ones. One interviewee talks of atten

item.title: ‘Reminds me of home’: why Coming to America is my feelgood movie
item.description: The latest in our series of writers picking their most rewatched comfort films is an ode to Eddie Murphy’s beloved culture-clash comedy “Good morning, my neighbors!” A young Eddie Murphy shouts from the balcony of a shady apartment building. In the bustling Queens neighborhood, he sticks out like a sore thumb with his foreign accent, tailored blazing jacket and red tie. “Hey, fuck you!” A voice yells from below and Murphy repeats the phrase, believing that it’s a greeting rather than an insult. It’s one of the standout scenes from the film Coming to America, because it’s so absurd but effective in that there is a cultural clash going on here. In Coming to America, Prince Akeem, played by Eddie Murphy, is the sole heir to the throne of Zamunda, a fictitious African country. Instead of having an arranged marriage, Prince Akeem exercises his autonomy and intends to find his own bride somewhere far away from the continent, much to his parents’ chagrin. item.title: Brioche armchairs, butter sculptures and edible chandeliers: meet the new food artists
item.description: Culinary artists are turning fashion shows and design fairs into a feast for the eyes A pretty Venetian chandelier featuring delicate pink flowers and cascading blue leaves hangs from a ceiling. A hazy, warm light radiates from its tulip bulbs. Suddenly, a woman reaches up and snaps off one of the flower stems, giggling as she begins to nibble it. Welcome to the weird and wonderful world of Laila Gohar . The Egyptian-born, New York-based artist is part of a new wave of culinary artists blurring the lines between sustenance and spectacle, and this troupe have quickly become a firm fixture at fashion parties and design fairs, turning dining into a phenomenon and delight. Gohar describes the chandelier , made entirely from hand-spun sugar (including the silver chain that suspended it) as her “favourite thing she has done in recent history”. It labours under a ghastly portmanteau name that simply jams together “list” and “article” but somehow carries a hint of the diminutive about it, which the listicle’s detractors would say is absolutely right: a chart – a Top 20 or 50 or 100 – with each entry warranting a brief paragraph of explication, they are reviled as a cheap, largely effortless way to fill space online. They are also astoundingly popular, particularly when the subject is music, perhaps because people were compiling rock and pop’s history into listicles decades before the internet came along. item.title: Adder Stone by Clare Clark review – the story of a drowned Welsh village
item.description: A real-life flooding becomes a flashpoint in this novel exploring family relationships, female liberation and the drive for Welsh independence In the author’s note accompanying her eighth novel, Adder Stone, Clare Clark recalls first learning how a lake in the Welsh valleys shrank during the drought of 1976 only to reveal an abandoned village underneath. As a child, Clark became obsessed with the idea, envisaging a sort of Welsh Pompeii – houses and lives frozen in time, buried beneath the water and the mud. Fifty years since that uncanny occurrence, Clark’s richly researched novel seeks to tell the story of that forgotten Welsh village: not abandoned by choice, but forcibly evicted in order to make way for a new reservoir needed to service Liverpool’s growing population. Clark charts how this event had a profound impact on individual lives, but also how it served as a flashpoint in the broader conversation around Welsh independence. Continue reading...

item.description: France have the chance to topple the Springboks in the Nations Championship decider, with their Six Nations rivals also shining this autumn Even if the official November Test window had now closed, as used to be the case, this would already have been a vintage European autumn. Whatever still awaits on the inaugural Nations Championship finals weekend, it has been a richly enjoyable few weeks for both diehard fans and floating voters, topped off by more seismic results and overflowing emotions in London and Dublin on Saturday. Those flocking to Twickenham had their money’s worth even before the game started, as Lewis Moody, fighting the good fight against motor neurone disease, stood shoulder to shoulder with England’s players as they faced up to the All Blacks’ haka. A r ecord-breaking 37-12 home win was then swiftly followed by Ireland defeating the world champion Springboks 20-17 to complete another resounding northern hemisphere double whammy. item.title: Is it true that … we only use 10% of our brains?
item.description: The idea that we access a fraction of our cognitive potential goes back decades, but does medical science agree? This idea really bugs Dr Mary Spiller , senior lecturer in the University of East London’s Department of Psychology and Human Development, who’s shocked by how prevalent it remains, despite being untrue. Spiller says the myth’s origins can partly be traced to the work of William James, one of the founders of modern psychology, working in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. He wrote: “We are making use of only a small part of our possible mental and physical resources.” Continue reading...

item.title: Dapper Liam and Noel, experimental Björk, and Bowie ‘cuddling himself’: Rankin reveals his never-before-seen shots of the stars
item.description: After some satirical experiments with the ‘disgusting’ AI, the photographer has returned to his first love with a book of contact sheets from his celebrity shoots. ‘I wish we could go back and stop everything changing,’ he says “I hate AI,” says Rankin. “A lot of people think I’m an evangelical twat about it, and I’m not. I think it’s disgusting. I think the people who run it are disgusting. They’ve made a massive gamble with humanity and society and culture.” His contempt may surprise anyone who’s familiar with Rankin’s substantial AI output. Ever since the artist Damien Hirst introduced him to the possibilities of generative AI in 2021, the British photographer has been going further down the rabbit hole. “I’m not somebody who likes to be critical about something without actually knowing about it,” he explains. “I’ve gone deep into trying to work it out.” Continue reading...

item.description: Leeds offer Chelsea a lesson, Newcastle’s summer recruits struggle and Jules Ahoka makes a name for himself What to make of Manchester United’s utterly torrid start under Mauricio Pochettino? To go glass half full as the new head coach had only three days to prepare the side for the trip to Anfield, the hope will be that time will cast the 4-0 humbling from Liverpool as the falsest of false starts. The glass-half-empty scenario, though, is that here was an XI packed with internationals that had zero clue how to sort out a dire beginning themselves. Leny Yoro’s very early red card may have been questionable but for the wall to evaporate and allow Dominik Szoboszlai’s subsequent free-kick to arrow home was damning evidence of how immature Pochettino’s new charges are. item.title: Nasa, please send me to the moon. Science says I’m the perfect crew member | Helen Pilcher
item.description: Women of my age have been training for this job for years – solving problems, defusing tensions, keeping everyone fed – and we absolutely smash it Nasa is hiring and I’m over the moon. The US space agency is recruiting its next cohort of astronauts to work on the lunar surface and “help write the next chapter of humanity’s greatest adventure”. Applications close on 3 December. This isn’t the only job I’ve been swooning over lately. I can’t tell you how many hours I’ve lost to posts about deliciously distant jobs: running the world’s southernmost post office in Antarctica, where staff double as penguin counters, or minding the Great Blasket island off the coast of County Kerry, where the northern lights sometimes shimmer over the North Atlantic. All of it bathed in a warm, rosy glow. In our always-on world, swapping the inbox for an island – or, for the truly frazzled, the moon – seems less like a job and more like a wellness retreat. item.title: The Boy and the Suit of Lights review – a sensitive portrait of an aspiring toreador in a changing Spain
item.description: Encouraged by his grandfather and single mother, the teen Borja dreams of a career that will end his family’s poverty, but the protesters are gathering strength Where last year’s bullfighting documentary Afternoons of Solitude by Albert Serra was a tightly trussed formalistic affair concerned by the question of style in the arena and in art, this Scottish-produced film is a looser, more social-realist approach to la corrida . Swerving a portrayal of the butchery itself, it focuses on the wider community significance of this tradition in the eastern Spanish city of Castellón, via the figure of aspiring teen toreador Borja. Supported by his harried, cigarillo-smoking single mother, Raquel, Borja hopes that wearing the sequined “suit of lights” will help lift his family out of poverty. item.title: Why I love Berlin in winter: ‘Christmas markets arrive in a blaze of twinkling lights’
item.description: The cold is legendary, but there’s hot chocolate and Glühwein to warm you up, plus crowd-free museums and galleries and cosy candlelit pubs One of the first things Berliners warned me about when I moved here in 2008 was the winters. They talked in hushed, conspiratorial tones about the harsh winds that blew in from the Russian steppes, temperatures of minus 15C and the horrors of frozen bike locks. Having survived 17 of these winters (and counting), and still no hospitalisations for frostbite to report, I can confirm that the warnings, although not necessarily untrue, are not the whole story. Although some Berlin winter days are cold, miserable and grey, they can also be charming, cheerful and chock-full of possibilities. No sooner has the temperature dropped, and the last yellow leaves see-sawed from the trees at the end of November, than the city’s Christmas markets assert themselves in a blaze of twinkling lights, aromatic grill smoke, candied nuts and warming cups of Glühwein. item.title: The truth about dying: hospice workers on what loved ones should know
item.description: Anna Gordon met hospice care workers across the UK, learning how dignity and choice help create meaningful moments for patients Most people in the UK actively avoid conversations about death and dying. They can be visibly uncomfortable when you raise the subject. When people try to talk about it, it tends to be euphemistically. This is a mistake, one that can stop you from making important choices for yourself or your loved ones. It can increase fear and misunderstanding about what death can look like, while open conversations can help to ease these feelings and bring a sense of calm, peace and, on occasion, even beauty to the event. Nobody really wants to think about Brexit any more, save for the original Brexiters, who seem delighted that Andy Burnham’s “reset” with the EU has given them an excuse to get the old gang back together. But arguments about whether the UK should rejoin the EU will reignite in parliament this week, as Burnham briefs MPs on the deal he agreed on Friday. That deal wasn’t so much a victory as the culmination of Keir Starmer’s incrementalist approach to UK-EU relations. Its core agreements haven’t been ratified by member states yet, and the EU won’t sign them off until Britain resolves a dispute over tuition fees for European students. item.title: Connecting with Britain’s unsung carers has allowed me to feel a deep compassion for my younger self | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
item.description: Looking after my brother when I was a child was challenging and life-affirming. Now we need to give the next generation of carers proper support As the years have passed, I have often observed that caring for another person is a responsibility that few human beings completely escape. “Hardly anyone gets off scot-free in this life,” I recently said to a friend, as we discussed our various loved ones and their care needs, the worry and the responsibilities. Whether it’s our children, siblings, friends or parents, some sort of care work is usually required of us on our life’s journey. Illness, disability, mental health issues, ageing, accidents and other vulnerabilities inevitably touch our lives. There are 5.8 million unpaid carers in the UK, but I suspect there are far more who don’t identify as such, yet regularly care for loved ones or neighbours by helping with bills, shopping, appointments or more personal tasks. item.title: A taste of Italy: Alessandro Giannatempo’s recipes for Amalfi-style ricotta and pear cake, and crocodile’s porridge
item.description: Sweet from top to toe: a creamy, southern Italian fruit and nut cake, and an almondy polenta porridge from the north Although I grew up in Emilia-Romagna, my family history spans the Italian peninsula. Inspired by my mixed upbringing, these recipes reflect the flavours of both southern and northern Italy. The Amalfi-style ricotta and pear cake, as the name suggests, is a nod to the southern coast of Salerno. Fresh ricotta is whipped with lemony pears and sandwiched between layers of nutty hazelnut cake. The crocodile’s porridge, named after a traditional Italian beverage made with milk and pear juice, combines northern ingredients such as polenta and amaro for a very cosy stovetop-made dessert – or breakfast, if you ask me! He was the global teenage heart-throb. Even Michael Jackson trailed behind him. He was 14 when his most famous song, Puppy Love, spent five weeks at No 1 in the UK. My sister had a huge poster of him on her bedroom wall. Then again, everybody’s sister had a poster of him on their bedroom wall. item.title: ‘What if joining the resistance got your friends executed?’ The chilling new films casting Nazi collaborators in a fresh light
item.description: For decades, films about Nazi-occupied Europe were all about the fearless resistance while despicable collaborators deserved all they got. So what’s behind the spate of movies portraying turncoats in a more sympathetic light? A young maid busies herself in a vast, high-ceilinged apartment, serving her master steaming coffee in fine china and polishing the hefty family silver, as she picks her way across the checkerboard parquet lit by stylish Poul Henningsen lamps. Woman Unknown , which won the Golden Lion at the Venice film festival this year, is set in the immediate aftermath of Denmark’s liberation from Nazi rule, but you wouldn’t know that from the opening scenes: five years of occupation, martial law and rationing have left the splendour of the Danish bourgeoisie miraculously untouched. The text they rejected barely recognised the catastrophic climate emergency we’re facing, let alone signalled a definitive move away from fossil fuels. The good news is that most of the world’s governments rejected an agreement stripped of meaning. And the power of one particular fossil fuel producer, Saudi Arabia, needs particular scrutiny. item.title: I stopped talking to my husband and let AI do it instead. He didn’t even notice | Polly Hudson
item.description: What have I learned from my experiment with outsourcing? That I’m easily replaced – and awful I’ve just ventured deeper into my phone’s settings than anybody has ever been before. A software update is always discombobulating, but the latest one brought a lot of unwanted AI nonsense (that mental image you just got of me waving my fist at the sky: spot on). Even when you manually switch off Apple Intelligence, check the box to make Siri the same dummy she’s always been, and deselect the option to offer replies to texts and emails, it makes no difference. Harrumph. Days later, bored on the bus, I began answering my husband’s texts with the terrible suggested AI responses, to see if he’d notice. (We’ve been married a long time; this is how I get my kicks now.) Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? item.title: Readers reply: when does a reasonable train route become unreasonable?
item.description: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions ponders a quirk of the UK railway system • This week’s question: is there any way in which ‘manifesting’ can achieve the desired effect? I recently made a return trip to Edinburgh from London on which both legs of the journey were either significantly delayed or cancelled. At Waverley station, a message over the public address system told us we could travel by any “reasonable” route, but what does that mean? What counts as reasonable and what doesn’t? And who decides? Grant, by email Send new questions to nq@theguardian.com . When a journey is between stations that have one or more common routeing points, the permitted journey takes the route of shortest distance or any route no more than 3 miles longer, whether or not they pass through the common routeing point. Also permitted are journeys that use direct trains to and from the common routeing point. Continue reading...

item.title: How can we explain psychosomatic illnesses?
item.description: Emotions play a significant part in physical symptoms – but not in the way people often imagine When Diego started seeing bright flashing lights in his field of vision and felt his legs go weak, he thought he knew immediately what was happening. His mother had a stroke in her 60s, and although Diego was active and (unlike his mother) didn’t smoke, he had always expected that the same would happen to him. So it was a huge relief to be told – after seeing a stroke specialist and having a brain scan – that he had not had a stroke at all. Unfortunately the relief was short-lived. The visual disturbances and the weakness were real and debilitating. If this wasn’t a stroke, what was it? Some illnesses aren’t caused by disease or damage, but arise when the coordinated functioning of the body goes awry. In a percentage of these cases a person’s psychological health is an important element in their symptoms. Intuitively this seems mysterious. We are accustomed to thinking about physical symptom

item.description: Former defender reflects on his record-breaking longevity, kicking Eden Hazard in training, and life after retirement César Azpilicueta looks well. César Azpilicueta always looks well – “ah, Captain Handsome,” one Chelsea fan says when told who’s turning up – but today especially, smiling in the sunshine. Strolling in, he eases into an easier chair, golf course spreading out beyond the terrace, west of Madrid, and orders a detox almost as green. It is nearly 20 years since he played his first game and a few months since he played his last, training kit replaced by bermudas, loafers and a polo, a picture of relaxation. So what’s it like not being a footballer? “Well, different,” he says. Then he laughs, which he does a lot. It is not a laugh-your-head-off laugh, more a chuckle, a giggle, as if amused at everything he did. And for all the self-deprecation, the lack of triumphalism, he did everything. item.description: I was bullied for my deafness as a child, and just when I was finding myself, a car crash set me back years. When I went to see Better Man, the 2024 biopic in which Williams is played by a CGI chimp, I was tagging along with my wife. To be honest, I was sceptical about the ape but tried to meet the film with an open mind. I wasn’t looking for anything in particular but what I found was something that seemed to explain my life. I was born two months premature in Winnipeg, Canada, in 1961, with severe hearing loss in both ears that wasn’t diagnosed until I was seven. In 1969 we moved to Woking in Surrey; my father left and my mother descended into alcoholism. Our parents were busy working two or three jobs,” says Errol “Barzy” Beaumont, a founder member of Baron Turbo Charge, Manchester’s long-running reggae sound system. “It was the records – Burning Spear, Bob Marley, Culture, that were telling us about our culture, which wasn’t on the school curriculum. item.title: The Guardian view on Jan van Eyck’s portraits: what it means to be human | Editorial
item.description: A tiny scar, bloodshot eyes and sagging jowls – it is the intimate details of these 15th-century masterpieces that make them so relatable today The word “human” may have been crowned the Cambridge dictionary’s word of 2026 , but its meaning is nowhere more manifest than in an exhibition of paintings from almost 600 years ago. Humanness is captured in every pore and wrinkle of all nine of Jan van Eyck ’s portraits, united for the first time by the National Gallery. The paintings have been loaned from Berlin, Vienna, Dresden, Bruges and Sibiu in Romania, in a triumph of cultural exchange that proves the blockbuster show is still very much alive. And so, it almost seems, are the people depicted in it, who appear so real we might “recognise them on the tube”, as the exhibition’s co-curator Nicholas Flory put it , even given their extravagant headgear. People in the US also don’t consume as wide a variety of mushrooms as other parts of the world, says Dr Krystle Zuniga, a board-certified oncology dietitian based in Austin, Texas. “I often think of them as a forgotten vegetable,” she says, though she clarifies they are technically fungi. item.title: ‘It gives me power’: the swimming class that’s changing lives
item.description: People who arrive in Australia not having learned to swim often fear the water. For these Splash of Colour Swimming students, even blowing bubbles ‘is Everest’ In a public pool in Melbourne’s west, where the smell of chlorine hangs thick in the air, Dharmveer Kaur practises blowing bubbles in the shallow pool. Sounds echo across the enormous indoor aquatic centre, as people fresh from school and work mingle in the pools, spas and water slides. Kaur quietly concentrates on submerging her face in the water, following her instructor’s guidance in a lane away from the chaos. To the young children taking swimming lessons in the lane beside her, the throngs of older men making their way to the spa, or the mother casually breastfeeding in the pool opposite her, Kaur’s bubble blowing may not seem remarkable. But for the woman who never learned to swim, it feels monumental. Continue reading...

item.title: Jodi Picoult: ‘Reading Ta-Nehisi Coates made me rethink racism’
item.description: The American novelist on the wild side of Maurice Sendak, re-evaluating Gone With the Wind, and the magical comforts of Alice Hoffman My favourite book growing up I loved Maurice Sendak’s Where the Wild Things Are. item.title: California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
item.description: Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years. Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. In the years since their last record, the band – and former member Robbie Williams – have indeed laid out the trials and tribulations of 35 years of Take That in several documentaries, some more candid than others. item.title: What history tells us about the Premier League table after 10 games of a season
item.description: Past years suggest it is tough to make big positional gains after slow start but that someone now safe will be relegated The Premier League is about to enter the most intense phase of its season. After 10 rounds of fixtures across the past three months there are 10 in the next seven weeks. Yet if you hibernated for winter, most clubs would be in roughly the same position no matter when in spring you emerged. Across the past decade, Premier League teams’ positions changed by an average of 2.6 places between matchweeks 10 and 38. Only 5.5 clubs per season moved by more than three places over the final 28 games, with almost half of the teams (89 out of 200) shifting by a single spot at most. Every club other than Arsenal will be looking to improve their position but they need not trouble themselves too much. History shows they will probably finish 2026-27 close to their current standing. Continue reading...

item.title: Summer signings join Lionel Messi among MLS’s top earners: Takeaways from the league’s salary release
item.description: How much in player salaries did it take to earn a point in the 2026 MLS regular season? The latest batch of salaries lends some insight Lionel Messi has closer company at the top of MLS’s list of highest-paid players, thanks to another pair of former Barcelona attackers. The Inter Miami captain is still comfortably the league’s top earner, on a guaranteed compensation of $28.3m. Robert Lewandowski (Chicago Fire) and Antoine Griezmann (Orlando City) have entered the list with the second and third highest wages, while Atlanta United’s Breel Embolo, another summer signing, ranks fifth on a guaranteed compensation of $10.8m. item.description: The journalist and broadcaster who died last week aged 69 knew the enduring power of radio, even as the landscape changed so quickly It’s injury time at the Emirates on 29 October 2008, Arsenal are 4-3 up against Tottenham. Tom Huddlestone cushions a ball to Luka Modric, whose strike takes a deflection. It loops over Manuel Almunia and off a post into the path of Aaron Lennon, who prods it home and starts skipping towards the Spurs supporters before diving on to the ground and being enveloped by Modric, Benoît Assou-Ekotto, Darren Bent and a couple of pitch-invading fans. Pandemonium, for once, seems the apt way to describe it. But the real entertainment is happening in a radio studio at 18 Hatfields, London SE1; the old home of TalkSport. As the goal goes in, a guttural voice makes an indecipherable but very loud noise. It’s hard to transcribe – perhaps “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH”, or maybe “OOEEERRAAGGH”. Instead, its strange anatomy appears to have been an extraordinary evolutionary adaptation for hunting along the seafloor.

item.description: Both launched in 2006, with contrasting visions of gaming – one focused on accessibility, the other on technical ambition – each leaving a lasting legacy • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The main focus of the games industry this week is, of course, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI – a game that could define the next decade for the industry. For this week’s newsletter though, I wanted to direct your attention two decades into the past. In November 2006, two console manufacturers launched their competing – and wildly different – visions of what the future of video games would look like. Twenty years later, it’s clear that somehow they were both right. And yet, in some ways, they were both wrong. item.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
item.description: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. item.description: The Russia-linked cyber espionage group known as Cold Relic (formerly COLDRIVER and UNC4057) has been observed weaponizing a single cloud compromise into a launchpad for a series of linked intrusions resulting in third-party compromise. Google's Mandiant and Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said it investigated a 2026 compromise at a U.S.-based organization in which the adversary leveraged

item.title: Can a US-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo?
item.description: The Lobito Corridor is at the centre of a US-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals.

item.title: Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K
item.description: Deep-sea researchers have captured stunning new footage of an extraordinarily rare fish with a transparent head and rotating eyes nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface. Known as the barreleye fish, this bizarre creature uses its upward-pointing eyes to spot prey before rotating them forward to track its next meal, all while a transparent dome protects them.

item.title: Tiny magnets deep inside the brain could transform Parkinson’s treatment
item.description: Scientists have developed a new technique that uses magnetic nanoparticles to stimulate deep brain regions, dramatically improving Parkinson’s-like movement problems in mice without permanently implanted electrodes. The breakthrough could pave the way for less invasive treatments using injectable particles and wearable magnetic headbands.

item.title: NASA pushes Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound
item.description: NASA has successfully tested Mars helicopter rotor blades at supersonic speeds, boosting potential lift by 30% and overcoming a major obstacle to more powerful aircraft on the Red Planet. The breakthrough could enable next-generation helicopters to carry heavier scientific equipment, fly farther, and explore places beyond the reach of traditional rovers.

item.title: Apple announces App Store price changes in multiple countries, new California tax rules
item.description: Apple today announced that App Store prices for apps and In-App Purchases will be adjusted in five countries starting December 3, following changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates. Here are the details. more…

item.title: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.
item.description: Scientists discovered that although people with and without autism show surprisingly similar average brain activity, individuals with autism exhibit much greater differences from one another, especially in regions involved in social understanding. The findings suggest that traditional research methods may be overlooking crucial differences that could help unlock more personalized autism support.

item.title: Kings of Leon to play at Apple Music Hall in December, tickets go on sale November 18
item.description: Apple Music Hall has added Kings of Leon to its lineup of upcoming gigs at the newly opened London venue. Here are the details. more…

item.title: Conference networking made simple, in three short videos
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03678-9 Working the room is a skill you can practise and prepare for. Here’s how.

item.title: First observation of a giant star swallowing its neighbour
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03784-8 Finding provides new insights into what happens within stellar mergers — plus, using quantum physics to securely pinpoint someone’s location.

item.title: How to make AI data centres more sustainable
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03708-6 Tech companies and governments face opposition over data centres’ expansion, in part because of their huge power requirements. They must not be powered with fossil fuels.

item.title: Microbiome home tests are taking off. Can they be trusted?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03710-y Our reporter mailed off her poo to find out what two companies say about her microbiome. Here’s what she found.

item.title: Tropical land-use intensification reshapes biodiversity in expected and unexpected ways
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03602-1 Global agricultural demand has increased over the past few decades, driving land-use intensification in some of the world’s most biodiverse regions. An assessment of some 40,000 species, from soil microorganisms to vertebrates, in Sumatra, Indonesia, reveals that agricultural intensification threatens biodiversity through species loss and changes in community composition across different spatial scales.

item.title: Kings of the jungle? This early human had surprising survival skills that rivalled ours
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03777-7 Teeth found in south China challenge the idea that Homo erectus lived only in woodlands and on savannahs.

item.title: Daily briefing: Can you spot the ‘tortured phrases’?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03791-9 Take Nature’s quiz to test your skills as a research-integrity sleuth. Plus, a milestone for Voyager 1 and the United States has lost its measles elimination status.

item.title: Intra-stellar: a star inside a giant star
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03273-y Long-term monitoring of a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy reveals, for the first time, the decay of the orbit of another star inside the giant’s envelope.

item.title: Glucose-powered implant brings devices for treating diabetes a step closer
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03377-5 A device that stimulates the main nerve between the brain and the internal organs when blood sugar is high is an effective therapy in rat models of diabetes.

item.title: Band-Edge-Extended Heterointerfaces for Perovskite Solar Cells and Tandems
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11427-1 Band-Edge-Extended Heterointerfaces for Perovskite Solar Cells and Tandems

item.title: Poxviruses probably evolved in the digestive system of animals
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03436-x Large and giant DNA viruses that infect unicellular eukaryotes are abundant in the environment but have rarely been found in the gut microbiome. The discovery of such viruses that prevail in the digestive system of humans and animals exposes a long-overlooked facet of the gut microbiome that clarifies the origin of poxviruses.

item.title: Meet ‘egoviruses’: the surprise microbes living in the guts of millions of people
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03766-w Egoviruses could be the evolutionary missing link between giant viruses that infect single-celled organisms and those that can infect people.

item.title: A new view of Amazonian leaf seasonality
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03490-5 Much of the Amazon rainforest was thought to be evergreen, but high-resolution satellite imagery reveals that many of its trees can remain leafless for longer than expected.

item.title: Injured locusts heal or are cannibalized depending on levels of a bacterial odour molecule
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03599-7 When migratory locusts are injured, an odorous chemical produced by bacteria living in or on their bodies activates the immune system, helping them to fight disease-causing agents. However, when a wound is large and the chemical becomes too concentrated, it attracts cannibalistic locusts.

item.title: Are you a budding science sleuth? Take our plagiarism quiz to test your skills
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03040-z Sleuths and publishers seize on ‘tortured phrases’ to detect research fraud. Sometimes they can raise a smile.

item.title: AI must be held accountable — value statements won’t protect human dignity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03717-5 Technology companies can’t be the judges of their own regulatory compliance. Centuries of history explain why.

item.title: A grant to hand out more grants — and build a research area
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03689-6 A rapid microgrants scheme called the Field Building Accelerator aims to launch new scientific fields.

item.title: Quantum physics can prove where you are
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03378-4 Demonstrating your location to someone far away is surprisingly hard. Quantum correlations offer a way to do so without needing to trust any quantum hardware.

item.title: The right to do wrong
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03517-x An equal chance.

item.title: Widespread deciduousness reveals diverse Amazonian phenological strategies
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11284-y A basin-wide assessment of Amazonian deciduousness using high-resolution satellite observations shows a diverse range of phenological strategies across the Amazon rainforest, contrary to the prevailing view of Amazonian phenology.

item.title: Observation of tunable superradiant frequency combs
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11289-7 A transition from continuous to periodic pulsed superradiant emission in coupled spin–resonator systems is demonstrated, revealing connections to time crystals and enabling synchronized microwave and optical frequency combs.

item.title: Rethinking corporate climate targets for real-world transitions
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11100-7 Frameworks for corporate greenhouse gas reduction targets should place greater emphasis on systemic changes in business models, technologies and value chains; the scientific community has a role in developing robust, actionable frameworks for corporate decarbonization.

item.title: Analogue simulation of massive relativistic quantum fields in 2 + 1 dimensions
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11268-y Analogue simulation of massive relativistic quantum fields in 2 + 1 dimensions (two spatial dimensions and time) is realized using two coherently coupled spin components in a two-dimensional atomic Bose–Einstein condensate.

item.title: A glucose-powered artificial neuroimmune axis for metabolic control
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11251-7 NeuroAxis restores glucose tolerance, improves insulin sensitivity and normalizes glycaemic control, with therapeutic effects persisting after treatment cessation in rat models of type 1 and type 2 diabetes.

item.title: Conservation of the tumour microenvironment across organs and species
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11270-4 A pan-cancer single-cell analysis of the tumour microenvironment across 42 cancer types and across 2 species is described.

item.title: Quantum position verification with remote untrusted devices
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11247-3 A loophole-free Bell-test quantum protocol demonstrates secure, device-independent position verification, achieving up to 4.53-fold smaller localization volumes than classical methods and enabling tamper-resistant location-based authentication.

item.title: Quantum resistance paradox of low-dimensional superfluids
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11294-w A defect-free unitary Fermi gas is used in a digitally programmable transport geometry to isolate geometric effects on superfluid dissipation and discover a paradox.

item.title: Fully integrated perovskite active polaritonic circuits
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11299-5 A fully integrated perovskite polaritonic circuit that brings the functionalities of fully integrated on-chip polaritonic systems simultaneously delivering room-temperature waveguide lasing, controllable optical routing and amplification together in a single-step-grown platform is shown.

item.title: TransA-MERFISH reveals divergent post-retinal direction-selective circuits
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11235-7 TransA-MERFISH combines anterograde trans-neuronal tracing and spatial transcriptomics and reveals distinct retinal on–off direction-selective ganglion cell-dependent and independent motion-selective pathways in superior colliculus, establishing a sensitive cell-type-resolved framework for wiring-diagram reconstruction in early visual processing.

item.title: Flat-band-induced integer doping and phase transition in monolayer graphene
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11254-4 An architecture comprising monolayer graphene doubly aligned to bulk and monolayer hBN on either side shows a gate-tunable global structural phase transition between two stacking configurations, accompanied by flat-band-induced integer doping.

item.title: Rainforest adaptation in late Homo erectus from southern China
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11155-6 Eight Homo erectus teeth from two caves in southern China reveal that the species persisted in closed rainforest ecosystems between 324 and 184 ka, challenging assumptions about their ecological preferences and behavioural limitations.

item.title: Bogong moths navigate with a light-dependent geomagnetic inclination compass
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11322-9 During their biannual migration, nocturnal Bogong moths (Agrotis infusa) rely on both a stellar and a geomagnetic compass for navigation, enabling them to maintain their migratory direction even if one of these cues is missing.

item.title: An inspiral of a star inside a common envelope with its giant companion
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11221-z Observations of AT 2025abao provide direct evidence of common-envelope inspiral, revealing frictional energy dissipation and constraining how orbital energy drives stellar-envelope ejection during binary evolution.

item.title: Global patterns and drivers of bee richness and endemism on islands
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11325-6 Gobal analysis of bee species across 305 islands reveals that islands account for 20% of global bee diversity, with more than 4,100 species and high levels of endemism, and shows that richness is shaped by island size, isolation and evolutionary diversification.

item.title: Host–microbe interactions in engineered immunocompetent human gut tissues
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11292-y Engineered barrier models of the small intestine and colon that include immune cells and a microbial compartment enable characterizations of the human epithelial response to Salmonella Typhimurium at the single-cell level.

item.title: Injury-induced signalling coordinates immunity and cannibalism in locusts
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11297-7 Studies in migratory locusts identify a dual role of volatile guaiacol emission, enhancing survival of individual insects following minor injury but attracting cannibalistic attack once an injury severity threshold has been exceeded.

item.title: Structural and regulatory evolution across the genus Hordeum
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11332-7 Chromosome-scale pangenomics across diploid Hordeum species reveals extensive structural variation, hybridization, introgression, horizontal gene transfer and regulatory evolution, revealing adaptive trait diversification and providing genomic resources for barley improvement.

item.title: Evidence for late Middle Pleistocene Homo erectus in mainland East Asia
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11271-3 Late Middle Pleistocene hominin teeth from the Naxian and Baxian caves of southern China, dated to around 324–184 thousand years ago, fill a gap in the geographical and chronological distribution of Homo erectus in East Asia.

item.title: Closest relatives of poxviruses prevail in human and animal guts worldwide
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11283-z A diversified group of DNA viruses with large linear genomes is discovered, egoviruses, that comprise a putative viral order most closely related to animal-infecting poxviruses, and prevail in the animal digestive system.

item.title: Evidence for p-wave magnetism in electronic band structure of metallic EuSi
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11295-9 A combination of symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations, neutron scattering and photoemission spectroscopy shows p-wave magnetism in the near-Fermi-level electronic structure of stoichiometric metallic EuSi.

item.title: Designing dislocation-driven polar vortex networks in twisted perovskites
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11330-9 Experimental and theoretical investigation of twisted freestanding SrTiO3 layers using various analytic methods from 4DSTEM to DFT reveal a long-range ordered screw dislocation pattern as well as topological polar vortex arrays in the interface plane.

item.title: Transient contacts between filaments impart its elasticity to branched actin
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11300-1 Stiffness of branched actin networks emerges from the formation of contacts between filaments, with growth under load resulting in stiffer networks.

item.title: Tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11298-6 Tropical land-use intensification drives substantial biodiversity loss and reorganizes community composition, with aboveground assemblages showing an increase in nestedness in monocultures compared with forests, underscoring the need for landscape-scale, multi-taxon conservation that integrates agricultural and natural habitats.

item.title: Ferroptosis in cancer cells triggers PGE<sub>2</sub> production for tumour immune escape
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11333-6 Ferroptotic cancer cells activate a molecular program that causes increased levels of PGE2, which in turn impairs type 1 conventional dendritic cell function, compromising antitumour CD8+ T cell immunity.

item.title: Hypothalamic volume and cell-type changes in ageing and Alzheimer’s disease
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11305-w HypoAD, an atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and Alzheimer’s disease that combines high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging from 458 individuals with single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 614,403 nuclei, reveals that metabolism- and circadian-regulating subregions, and their inhibitory neurons and microglia, are particularly vulnerable.

item.title: Reliving the drama: England and Argentina stars watch 1986 classic with fresh eyes
item.description: A new film about the historic World Cup quarter-final clash finds new angles for a new generation “Is there anything new to say about it?” Gary Lineker asked the producer Flora Fernandez-Marengo when she first approached him to take part in The Match, a documentary about the 1986 World Cup quarter-final between England and Argentina. Maradona wearing a union jack T-shirt and Freddie Mercury an Argentina strip. It worked. Lineker said yes. The rock’n’roll angle, with Brian May as a talking head, is one of the very few details the film-makers added to Andrés Burgo’s book, The Match, on which the documentary is based. item.title: Janine van Wyk: ‘Our rooms were empty … no mattresses, no lightbulbs and not a drop of water’
item.description: In an extract from the former South Africa captain’s book, she details less than ideal Wafcon 2006 preparations I was just a year into my international career when we qualified for my first Wafcon, which was then called the African Women’s Championship (AWC) and was held in Nigeria in 2006. I was extremely excited but very nervous to participate in this tournament, more so when it was announced that we would be in the same group as the hosts, and would play them last in the group. As it turned out, it would be the game that decided who finished top of the group. By then we had beaten Algeria 4-0 and Equatorial Guinea 2-0 and had to travel to Delta State to take on the hosts. I’d heard that Nigeria was the toughest country to travel to and I was about to realise why. It’s become common knowledge that South Africans and Nigerians are massive rivals on the football field but also don’t really get on off it. Continue reading...

item.title: Ozempic and Mounjaro may have a surprising effect on your brain
item.description: Blockbuster weight loss drugs like Ozempic and Mounjaro may do more than help people shed pounds, with growing evidence suggesting they could also influence brain health. Although studies have linked GLP-1 medications to a lower risk of dementia, major trials found that semaglutide did not slow Alzheimer's disease. Scientists suspect these drugs may be more effective at preserving memory and thinking abilities in people with obesity or diabetes, especially before cognitive problems appear.

item.title: Echoes of Azteca but not like Argentina: fearless England start afresh in Madrid
item.description: ‘We will not go back on this way of playing,’ says Thomas Tuchel after he delivered response to World Cup critics Thomas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead. He finished with three centre-backs on the pitch. His team could not get out of their half in the final part of the game. So close your eyes and imagine an alternate universe in which James Trafford did not make his stunning double save in stoppage time on Sunday and England had drawn 3-3 with Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium rather than won 3-2 . The reaction would not have been kind because Tuchel has been here before. The head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer. “It was Mexico reloaded,” he said, with a nod towards the 3-2 last-16 win at the Azteca Stadium and it fitted like a glove – down to the detail of Jarell Quansah and red cards. Emslie, a Scotland international who also plays as a forward for Angel City FC , documented her journey through pregnancy and football training on social media and is part of a growing number of professional female footballers who are getting pregnant in their athletic prime and approaching motherhood with a fresh mindset. Rather than marking the end of a career (notably, Millie Bright announced her pregnancy in September, months after having retired), pregnancy can mark both a continuation and a renewal. item.title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: this season’s big idea? Wear a skirt. It’s that simple
item.description: All you need to look on-trend this autumn is a skirt, but instead of going shopping, check what you already have in your wardrobe I go to a lot of fashion shows, and sometimes they are gorgeous and sometimes they are ugly. Sometimes they are electrifying and sometimes they are deathly dull. Sometimes they are completely baffling. My absolute favourite kind of show is the one that makes me want to run home and change my outfit. A show that makes me think: there it is! That’s exactly what I want to wear. When the look speaks to me, as if it had been on the tip of my tongue. God, I love that. Which is what happened at Prada this season . The idea was: skirts. That’s it, that’s the whole idea. The show was 63 different skirts – some with a sweater, some with a bra top, some with a jacket, but the point was the skirts. They were knee-length, give or take an inch up or down, and A-line, although sometimes a narrow almost-pencil and other times with a broader flare. There were skirts that wra

item.description: Plus: more speedy marathons by footballers, headed goals of the season and chairs acting as managers Mail us with all of your questions and answers “Which club team has had the most international captains playing together at one time?” asks MH Zahid. “Conversely, which international team has had the most club captains in its starting lineup at one time?” A quick web search finds a fuss being made in various corners of the internet of Chelsea’s 2009-10 squad because it contained six national team captains in Michael Ballack (Germany), Petr Cech (Czech Republic), Didier Drogba (Côte d’Ivoire), Branislav Ivanovic (Serbia), Mikel John Obi (Nigeria) and John Terry (England). These are, indeed, six people who captained their countries, playing together at one time, but crucially they were not all international captains at that time, which because we like to have our hands bound as tight as possible – no questions please – mean they are disqualified from this particular tournament. item.title: Ultimate 1-50: the male footballers best associated with each squad number
item.description: Who is football’s most legendary No 9? Has there ever been a legendary No 28? And why exactly does Mario Balotelli love wearing No 45 so much? Here’s our list and the stories behind it The relationship between players and numbers is a long-established one filled with memories and fascinating as well as fun stories behind them. With that in mind, the Guardian has had a go at deciding which male player is best associated with each squad number, from 1-50. Various factors were taken into consideration, including how long a player wore/has worn that number, what they achieved/have achieved in it, why they decided to wear it in the first place and, in some cases, how distinctly it has become associated with them in death. The below list is highly subjective and ultimately a bit of fun, but don’t let that stop you being shocked and furious in equal measure. *** Continue reading...

item.title: Football comes together across Spain to honour Jesús de Miguel: ‘We’ve seen how fragile life is’
item.description: Across La Liga and beyond this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them In the final few minutes before stepping into the arena once more, heading out for his 199th Osasuna match on Saturday evening, the man who has scored more first division goals than anyone in their history stopped his teammates for a moment and told them what it meant to wear the shirt. “This is very important,” Ante Budimir began as the dressing room, their sanctuary, fell silent around him. “We don’t have this shirt today for the sake of it. He was not chosen, and nor are we. It could have happened to anyone, anyone. Let us go knowing that we’re grateful to be on the pitch: playing, watching, warming up, sitting on the bench, whatever it may be. Boys, we were not chosen: not us, not him. Let us go, gratefully. item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...
